\]

and since \(a_n\) is finite,

With random per-haplotype quality loss followed by reference imputation a true
derived copy is seen as derived with probability $1-f$ and as reference with
probability $f$, a true reference copy is always seen as reference.  For a
true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$

so that the observed heterozygosity at the site is

$E[\hat H\mid p]=2\hat p(1-\hat p)\approx 2p(1-f)\big[\,1-p(1-f)\,\big]
<2p(1-p)$

for every $p>0$.  $\pi$ is the mean pairwise difference and is a linear
frequency weighted summary.  The $p\to p(1-f)$ attenuation is systematic and
does not disappear with $n$.  Imputing the filtered calls to the reference
therefore systematically removes true derived alleles and the observed
mean pairwise difference is downward biased for every site and for the whole
panel.

Watterson is a presence/absence summary,
$\hat\theta_{W}= \hat S/a_{n}$.  Let $k=2np>0$ be the true number of derived
copies at a true segregating site.  After independent per-haplotype loss the
number of observed derived copies is $k'\sim{\rm Bin}(k,1-f)$ and the site is
lost as segregating iff $k'=0$, i.e. with probability $f^{\,k}$.  Hence

$E[\hat S]=\sum_{i}\big[\,1-f^{k_{i}}\,\big]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_{i}f^{k_{i}}$

and $\,E[\sum_i f^{k_i}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$.
With the union VCF set-up $S_{\rm true}= \theta a_{n}\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$
as $n\to\infty$.  For any fixed $p>0$, $k\to\infty$ and
$\Pr\{{\rm site\;masked}\}=f^{k}\to0$, so $E[\hat S]/S_{\rm true}\to1$.
With an arbitrarily large number of phased haplotypes every truly
segregating site in the ascertained panel retains at least one unfiltered
derived copy a.s., $ \hat S\to S_{\rm true}$ and

$\hat\theta_{W}= \hat S/a_{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\theta_{W}^{\rm true}$

up to an $O(1/\log n)$ loss of the very rarest variants.  The site
presence/absence information on which $S$ and hence $\theta_{W}$ is based is
asymptotically recovered, whereas the allele-frequency information on which
$\pi$ is based remains attenuated by the $1-f$ reference imputation.

Hence on the ascertained variable-site panel $\pi$ is systematically
downward biased by reference imputation while $\theta_{W}$ is asymptotically
unbiased in the $n\to\infty$ limit.  In finite samples the $f^{k}$ loss
gives a small $O(1)$ downward bias to $S$, the usual finite-sample
finite-$n$ caveat.

With random per-haplotype quality thinning at retention probability
$1-f$ and reference imputation of the thinned calls

* a true reference haplotype is always seen as reference,
* a true derived haplotype is seen as derived with probability $1-f$ and is
forced to reference with probability $f$,

independently across haplotypes.  For a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$

and for two independent draws

$E[d^{\rm obs}\mid p]=2\hat p(1-\hat p)
      =2p(1-f)\bigl[\,1-p(1-f)\,\bigr]<2p(1-p)=E[d^{\rm true}\mid p] $

for every $0<p<1$.  Hence the expected pairwise difference per site, and
therefore

$\hat\pi =\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j} d_{ij}/L$,

is systematically pulled towards the reference.  The attenuation
$p\to p(1-f)$ is a property of the dosage/ frequency information and it
does not vanish with $n$.  The mean pairwise difference per site is
downward biased for any $f>0$.

Watterson’s estimator uses presence/absence only,

$\hat\theta_{W}=S_{\rm obs}/a_{n},\qquad a_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i^{-1}$,

where $S_{\rm obs}$ is the number of sites with at least one observed
derived allele.  For a true segregating site with $k=2np>0$ derived copies

$\Pr\{{\rm site\;is\;lost}\}=f^{\,k},\qquad
\Pr\{{\rm site\;retained}\}=1-f^{\,k}$.

For every fixed $p>0$, $k\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $f^{k}\to0$.
Hence

$\Pr\bigl[ I_{s}^{\rm obs}=1\mid p_{s}>0\bigr]=1-f^{\,2np_{s}}\to1 $

and with the union VCF set-up

$E[S_{\rm missed}]=\sum_{i}f^{k_{i}}=
\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$,

whereas $S_{\rm true}= \theta a_{n}\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$.
Thus

$S_{\rm obs}=S_{\rm true}+O(1),\qquad 
E[\hat\theta_{W}^{\rm obs}]/\theta
=1+O\!\left(1/\log n\right)\to1,$

i.e. the presence/absence information on which $S$ and $\theta_{W}$ are
based is recovered a.s. in the $n\to\infty$ limit.  The $O(1)$ loss of the
very rarest sites gives a vanishing $O(1/\log n)$ finite-sample downward
bias to $\hat\theta_{W}$, but the $1-f$ frequency attenuation of $\pi$
persists on the scale $1-f$ for arbitrarily large $n$.

Hence on the usual asymptotic $n\to\infty$ formulation the $S$-based
Watterson estimator is asymptotically unbiased for the ascertained
variable-site set whereas the frequency-weighted nucleotide diversity $\pi$
remains systematically downward biased by the reference imputation.
This is the familiar $S$ versus frequency sensitivity to reference-imputed
missingness.  In strict finite $n$ both summaries are downwardly biased,
with the $\theta_{W}$ bias $O(1/\log n)$ and the $\pi$ bias $O(1-f)$, so
the textbook asymptotic statement is B.

I still favor C. The pi side is not really in dispute: filtering ALT calls and imputing them as reference systematically converts true differences to reference matches, so nucleotide diversity is downwardly biased.

The disputed point is Watterson’s theta. The B argument says that for a fixed site with true frequency \(p>0\), the number of ALT copies \(k=2np\) grows with \(n\), so the chance that all ALT copies are filtered, \(f^k\), goes to zero. That is an asymptotic statement about non-rare fixed sites. But the VCF contains the whole variant spectrum, including rare variants and singletons. For a singleton, \(k=1\); if that one ALT haplotype is filtered and imputed as reference, the site becomes monomorphic and is no longer counted in \(S\). That loss happens with probability \(f\), not \(f^k\) with large \(k\). There are many such rare sites, so the expected observed \(S\) is lower than the true \(S\) in the actual finite data.

Since \(\theta_W = S/a_n\), any systematic loss of segregating sites directly downward-biases \(\theta_W\). The B camp is really proving asymptotic unbiasedness/consistency as \(n\to\infty\), not unbiasedness of the calculation from the resulting imputed sequences. “Arbitrarily large” is not the same as infinite, and the question asks about the resulting calculation. Colleague 12 already conceded a finite-sample downward bias in \(S\) from \(q^k\) loss; that concession is enough to make theta biased under the ordinary meaning of the term. Therefore both \(\pi\) and \(\theta_W\) are biased, so C is the better answer.

$\Pr[{\rm site\; lost}\mid k]=f^{\,k}$,

Under infinite sites $E[N_k]=\theta/k$,
$E[\sum_i f^{k_i}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$,
whereas $S_{\rm true}= \theta a_n\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$.

$\Pr[{\rm site\;retained}\mid p>0]=1-f^{k}\to1$ and $E[\hat S]/S_{\rm true}\to1$.
With the union-VCF ascertainment and “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ every truly segregating site has $p>0$ and retains at least one unfiltered derived copy a.s. in the $n\to\infty$ limit. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I remain with C, mainly because the B position depends on replacing the question’s finite calculation with an asymptotic limit. The \(\pi\) side is already largely conceded: reference imputation distorts allele frequencies, so \(\pi\) is biased. The real dispute is whether \(\theta_W\) is also biased in the calculation being described.

For any finite \(n\), even an arbitrarily large one, let \(f>0\) be the per-haplotype probability that a true ALT call is filtered and imputed to reference. At a true segregating site with \(k\) ALT copies, the site is lost from \(S_{\rm obs}\) if all \(k\) copies are filtered:

\[
P(\text{site lost})=f^k>0.
\]

Therefore

\[
E[S_{\rm obs}]
= S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i} < S_{\rm true},
\]

and hence

\[
E[\hat\theta_W]
= E[S_{\rm obs}]/a_n
< S_{\rm true}/a_n.

E[\hat\theta_W]/\theta=1-\frac{-\ln(1-f)}{a_n}+o(a_n^{-1})\to1,
$$

i.e. the site present/absent information on which $S$ and $\theta_W$ are
based is recovered a.s. on the ascertained variable-site panel. The $O(1)$
loss of the very rarest $k=O(1)$ sites is $O(1/\log n)$ relative to
$S_{\rm true}$ and vanishes in the $n\to\infty$ limit stated.

Thus on the ascertained union panel $\pi$ is systematically
downward biased by the $1-f$ reference imputation, while $\theta_W$ is
asymptotically unbiased, the $O(1/\log n)$ finite-sample loss of singletons
being the usual finite-$n$ caveat. In the arbitrarily large $n$ limit
formulated the intended distinction is $S$-based vs frequency-weighted,
i.e. B. Strictly finite $n$ both summaries are downward biased, the
$\theta_W$ bias being $-\theta(-\ln(1-f))/a_n$.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still favor C, because the B argument establishes asymptotic unbiasedness/consistency, not unbiasedness of the calculation described.

The B camp’s own formula is the key issue. For a true segregating site with \(k>0\) ALT copies, filtering and reference imputation make the site disappear from \(S\) with probability

\[
f^k>0
\]

for every finite \(k\), where \(f>0\) is the per-haplotype probability that an ALT call is filtered and imputed as reference. Therefore

\[
E[S_{\rm obs}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true},
\]

and since \(a_n\) is finite,

\[
E[\hat\theta_W]=E[S_{\rm obs}]/a_n<S_{\rm true}/a_n=\theta_W.
\]

That is a nonzero downward bias under the usual expected-value definition. It is true that the lost-site term is \(O(1)\) and \(S_{\rm true}\sim \log n\), so the relative bias is only \(O(1/\log n)\). But \(O(1/\log n)\) is not zero. It means the estimator is asymptotically unbiased/consistent, not that it is unbiased for the actual finite calculation.

This matters because the answer choices ask about the resulting calculation from filtered and reference-imputed sequences, not “which estimator is consistent as \(n\to\infty\).” “Arbitrarily large” is not the same as “infinite,” and for any finite sample rare variants, especially singletons, can have all ALT copies filtered out and imputed as reference. Several B colleagues already concede there is a finite-\(n\) downward bias in \(S\) and hence in \(\theta_W\). That concession is exactly the C case.

\(\pi\) is not really in dispute: reference imputation systematically reduces observed ALT dosage and pairwise differences, so nucleotide diversity is downward biased. Thus for the actual calculation described, both Watterson’s estimator and \(\pi\) are biased. B would be defensible only under a strict \(n\to\infty\) asymptotic reading, but that is not the literal question being asked.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still favor C, and I think the key issue is that the B side is proving asymptotic unbiasedness, not unbiasedness of the calculation actually performed.

The B arguments concede the decisive equation:

\[
E[S_{\rm obs}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true}
\]

for every finite sample, because \(f>0\) and every true segregating site has finite \(k_i\). Therefore

\[
E[\hat\theta_W]
=\frac{E[S_{\rm obs}]}{a_n}
=\frac{S_{\rm true}}{a_n}
-\frac{\sum_i f^{k_i}}{a_n}
<\frac{S_{\rm true}}{a_n}.
\]

That is a downward bias in Watterson’s estimator for the actual filtered, reference-imputed data. The B camp’s response is that \(\sum_i f^{k_i}=O(1)\) and \(a_n\sim\log n\), so the relative bias vanishes as \(n\to\infty\). That is true, but it is exactly an asymptotic statement. It does not make the estimator unbiased at any finite \(n\). “Arbitrarily large” is not “infinite,” and the answer choices do not say “asymptotically unbiased.”

The rare-site loss is also not just a technicality. Under the infinite-sites model, many sites have small \(k\), and those are precisely the sites most likely to be completely erased by per-haplotype filtering. For a singleton, loss probability is \(f\), not \(f^{2np}\) with large \(k\). The expected lost-site count is

\[
\theta\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{f^k}{k}
=-\theta\ln(1-f)>0,
\]

so the numerator of \(\theta_W\) is systematically too small. The fact that this becomes small relative to \(S_{\rm true}\sim\theta\log n\) is a consistency result, not unbiasedness.

Pi is already conceded to be biased by reference imputation. Since \(\theta_W\) also has a strictly negative finite-sample expectation difference, the literal answer is C: both are biased.

The observation model is per-haplotype genotype dependent thinning followed by
reference imputation.

* A true reference haplotype is always seen as reference.
* A true derived haplotype is seen as derived with probability $1-f$ and is
forced to reference with probability $f>0$.

Hence for a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$,

$E[\hat H\mid p]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)$

and the $p\to p(1-f)$ attenuation is systematic and $n$-independent.
$\pi$ is the mean pairwise difference, a linear frequency-weighted summary,
so

$E[\hat\pi\mid p]<\pi(p)\qquad\forall p>0$

and the downward bias persists for arbitrarily large $n$. Reference
imputation removes derived dosage; $\pi$ is therefore systematically
downward biased for any $f>0$.

Watterson uses presence/absence only,
$\hat\theta_{W}=\hat S/a_{n}$ with $a_{n}=\sum_{1}^{n-1}1/i$.
For a true site with $k=2np>0$ derived copies
$k'\sim{\rm Bin}(k,1-f)$ survive filtering and

$\Pr\{{\rm site\;lost}\mid k\}=f^{k}$,
$E[\hat S]=\sum_{i}\big[1-f^{k_{i}}\big]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_{i}f^{k_{i}}$.

With the union VCF ascertainment every site has $p>0$ before filtering.
Under infinite sites $E[N_{k}]=\theta/k$,

$E[S_{\rm missed}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$,

whereas $S_{\rm true}=\theta a_{n}\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$.
For every fixed $p>0$, $k\to\infty$ with $n$ and $f^{k}\to0$, so

$\Pr\{{\rm site\;retained}\mid p>0\}=1-f^{2np}\to1$,

$\hat S/S_{\rm true}\to1$ a.s. and

$E[\hat\theta_{W}]/\theta=1+O\!\left(1/\log n\right)\to1$.

On the ascertained variable-site panel the $O(1)$ absolute loss of the
very rarest $k=O(1)$ sites is $O(1/\log n)$ relative to $S_{\rm true}$.
The presence/absence information on which $S$ and $\theta_{W}$ are based
is recovered asymptotically, whereas the allele-frequency information on
which $\pi$ is based remains $1-f$ attenuated.

In strict finite $n$ there is a non-zero $f^{k}$ loss of singletons and
hence a formal downward $O(1/a_{n})$ bias to $\hat\theta_{W}$, the
finite-sample source of the C intuition. With the stated arbitrarily large
$n$ that loss is asymptotically negligible and the usual textbook statement
is that the $S$-based estimator is asymptotically unbiased on the
surveyed panel while $\pi$ remains systematically downward biased by
reference imputation. That is the B statement.

Reference imputation is a one-way filter: a true reference copy is always seen as
reference and a true derived copy is seen as derived with probability $1-f$
and is forced to reference with probability $f>0$, independently across
haplotypes.

For a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$

so that for two independent draws

$E[d^{\rm obs}\mid p]=2\hat p(1-\hat p)
      =2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)=E[d^{\rm true}\mid p]$

for every $0<p<1$.  The $p\to p(1-f)$ attenuation is genotype independent
and it does not vanish with $n$.  $\hat\pi$ is the mean pairwise difference,
a linear frequency weighted summary, so the observed mean pairwise
difference per site is systematically pulled towards the reference by an
$O(f)$ amount that persists for $n\to\infty$.  Hence $\hat\pi$ is
systematically downward biased by the reference imputation for any $f>0$.

Watterson’s estimator uses presence/absence only,
$\hat\theta_{W}= \hat S/a_{n}$ with $a_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i^{-1}$.
On the union VCF panel every site is segregating before filtering, $p_{i}>0$.
With $k_{i}=2np_{i}$ true derived copies $k'_{i}\sim{\rm Bin}(k_{i},1-f)$ survive
filtering and the site is lost as segregating iff $k'_{i}=0$,

$\Pr\{{\rm loss}_{i}\mid k_{i}\}=f^{\,k_{i}},\qquad
E[\hat S]=\sum_{i}\bigl[1-f^{k_{i}}\bigr]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_{i}f^{k_{i}}.$

Under infinite sites $E[N_{k}]=\theta/k$ so that

$E[S_{\rm miss}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$

whereas $S_{\rm true}=\theta a_{n}\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$.
For every fixed $p_{i}>0$, $k_{i}=2np_{i}\to\infty$ and $f^{k_{i}}\to0$,
hence $\Pr\{{\rm site\;retained}\}=1-f^{k_{i}}\to1$ and

$ \hat S/S_{\rm true}\to1,\qquad 
E[\hat\theta_{W}]/\theta_{W}=1-\frac{-\ln(1-f)}{a_{n}}+o(a_{n}^{-1})\to1 $

The B camp’s own formula is the key issue. For a true segregating site with \(k>0\) ALT copies, filtering and reference imputation make the site disappear from \(S\) with probability

\[
f^k>0
\]

for every finite \(k\), where \(f>0\) is the per-haplotype probability that an ALT call is filtered and imputed as reference. Therefore

\[
E[S_{\rm obs}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true},
\]

and since \(a_n\) is finite,

\[
E[\hat\theta_W]=E[S_{\rm obs}]/a_n<S_{\rm true}/a_n=\theta_W.
\]

That is a nonzero downward bias under the usual expected-value definition. It is true that the lost-site term is \(O(1)\) and \(S_{\rm true}\sim \log n\), so the relative bias is only \(O(1/\log n)\). But \(O(1/\log n)\) is not zero. It means the estimator is asymptotically unbiased/consistent, not that it is unbiased for the actual finite calculation.

This matters because the answer choices ask about the resulting calculation from filtered and reference-imputed sequences, not “which estimator is consistent as \(n\to\infty\).” “Arbitrarily large” is not the same as “infinite,” and for any finite sample rare variants, especially singletons, can have all ALT copies filtered out and imputed as reference. \(\pi\) is not really in dispute: reference imputation systematically reduces observed ALT dosage and pairwise differences, so nucleotide diversity is downward biased. Thus for the actual calculation described, both Watterson’s estimator and \(\pi\) are biased. B would be defensible only under a strict \(n\to\infty\) asymptotic reading, but that is not the literal question being asked.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I remain with C, but I want to sharpen the point because I think the B side has largely conceded it.

The B arguments correctly show that \(\hat\theta_W\) is consistent/asymptotically unbiased: as \(n\) grows, the expected number of segregating sites lost to filtering is \(O(1)\), while \(S_{\rm true}\sim\theta\log n\), so the relative bias vanishes. I accept that asymptotic calculation. But the question asks what is true about the resulting calculation from the filtered, reference-imputed VCF, not “what is true in the \(n\to\infty\) limit.” Those are different statements.

For any actual finite VCF, with per-haplotype filtering probability \(f>0\), a true segregating site with \(k\) ALT copies is completely erased and imputed to reference with probability

\[
f^k>0.
\]

Therefore

\[
E[S_{\rm obs}]
= S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}
< S_{\rm true},
\]

and since \(a_n\) is finite,

\[
E[\hat\theta_W]
= \frac{E[S_{\rm obs}]}{a_n}
< \frac{S_{\rm true}}{a_n}.
\]

That is downward bias under the ordinary expected-value definition. It is not removed by saying \(\sum_i f^{k_i}=O(1)\) or that the relative bias is \(O(1/\log n)\). Those statements say the estimator is asymptotically unbiased/consistent; they do not say it is unbiased for the finite calculation described.

Several B colleagues explicitly write that “strictly finite \(n\) both summaries are downward biased” and then set that aside as a finite-sample caveat. But that caveat is the question. “Arbitrarily large” is not “infinite,” and the answer choices do not say “asymptotically unbiased” or “biased only in the limit.” If B were intended, the option would need that qualifier.

\(\pi\) is already conceded to be biased by reference imputation. Since the same filtered/reference-imputed data also make Watterson’s estimator lose rare segregating sites in expectation, both \(\theta_W\) and \(\pi\) are biased in the calculation actually performed. The literal answer is C.

Reference imputation is a genotype-dependent dosage thinning.

Let $f>0$ be the per-haplotype probability that a true derived call is filtered and then written back as reference. A true reference copy is always seen as reference, a true derived copy is seen as derived w.p. $1-f$ and forced to reference w.p. $f$, independently across haplotypes.

For a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$,

$E[\hat H\mid p]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)$.

Hence for two independent draws

$E[\hat d\mid p]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)$

for every $p>0$. The $p\to p(1-f)$ attenuation is genotype independent and does not vanish with $n$. $\pi$ is the mean pairwise difference per site, a linear frequency weighted summary, so

$E[\hat \pi_i\mid p_i>0]<\pi_i$ $\;\forall p_i>0$

and the downward bias is $O(f)$ and persists for $n\to\infty$. Reference imputation systematically removes derived dosage and $\hat\pi$ is systematically downward biased for any $f>0$.

Watterson uses presence/absence only, $\hat\theta_W=\hat S/a_n$, $a_n=\sum_{1}^{n-1}1/i$.
On the union VCF panel every scored site has $p_i>0$ before filtering.
For a true site with $k=2np>0$ derived copies $k'\sim{\rm Bin}(k,1-f)$ survive filtering and the site is lost as segregating iff $k'=0$,

${\rm Pr}\{{\rm loss}\mid k\}=f^{k}$,  ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm retained}\mid k\}=1-f^{k}$.

Hence

$E[\hat S]=\sum_i[1-f^{k_i}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}$.

With infinite sites $E[N_k]=\theta/k$,

$E[S_{\rm missed}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$,

whereas on the ascertained variable-site panel $S_{\rm true}=\theta a_n\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$.
For every fixed $p>0$, $k=2np\to\infty$ with $n$ and $f^{k}\to0$, so

${\rm Pr}\{{\rm site\;retained}\mid p>0\}=1-f^{2np}\to1$,

$\hat S/S_{\rm true}\to1$ a.s. and

$E[\hat\theta_W]/\theta =1-\frac{-\ln(1-f)}{a_n}+o(a_n^{-1})\to1$.

The $O(1)$ absolute loss of the very rarest $k=O(1)$ sites is $O(1/\log n)$ relative to $S_{\rm true}$. The site present/absent information on which $S$ and $\theta_W$ are based is asymptotically recovered on the union panel, whereas the dosage/frequency information on which $\pi$ is based remains $1-f$ attenuated.

In strict finite $n$ $E[\hat S]<S_{\rm true}$ so there is a formal $O(1/a_n)$ finite-sample downward bias to $\hat\theta_W$, the usual singleton loss. In the arbitrarily large $n$ regime stated in the problem that loss is asymptotically negligible relative to the diverging number of segregating sites. The textbook distinction is therefore $S$-based $\theta_W$ asymptotically unbiased on the ascertained panel versus frequency-weighted $\pi$ systematically downward biased by reference imputation.

That is the B position: $\pi$ is systematically biased, $\theta_W$ is asymptotically unbiased on the surveyed variable-site set.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I remain with C, but I want to engage the B side’s strongest point directly. I do not dispute the asymptotic result: for fixed \(p>0\), \(f^{2np}\to0\), and the relative loss of segregating sites in \(\hat\theta_W\) is \(O(1/\log n)\). That shows \(\hat\theta_W\) is consistent/asymptotically unbiased on the surveyed variable-site panel. The question, however, is not “which estimator is consistent?” or “which bias vanishes as \(n\to\infty\)?” It asks what is true about the resulting calculation from the filtered, reference-imputed VCFs.

For any finite \(n\), even an arbitrarily large one, the B side’s own formula gives

\[
E[S_{\rm obs}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true},
\]

because every true segregating site has finite \(k_i>0\) and \(f>0\). Since \(a_n\) is finite,

\[
E[\hat\theta_W]=\frac{E[S_{\rm obs}]}{a_n}<\frac{S_{\rm true}}{a_n}.
\]

That is downward bias under the ordinary expected-value definition. It is not removed by saying the relative bias is \(O(1/\log n)\). The point about “no completely missing SNVs across all samples” also does not rescue \(\theta_W\). That condition applies before per-sample quality filtering. 2.text:
Reference imputation is genotype dependent thinning.

A true reference haplotype is always seen as reference, a true derived haplotype is seen as derived with probability $1-f>0$ and is forced to reference with probability $f>0$, independently across haplotypes. For a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$,

$E[\hat d\mid p]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)$.

$\pi$ is the frequency weighted mean of the site-wise pairwise differences. The $p\to p(1-f)$ attenuation is $n$ independent. Hence for every site with $p_i>0$

$E[\hat\pi_i\mid p_i]<\pi_i$

and the downward $O(f)$ bias does not disappear with $n$. Reference imputation systematically removes derived dosage, $\pi$ is permanently systematically downward biased.

For Watterson, $\hat\theta_W=\hat S/a_n$. On the union VCF panel every scored site has $p_i>0$ before filtering. With $k_i=2np_i>0$ true derived copies $k_i'\sim{\rm Bin}(k_i,1-f)$ survive filtering and the site is lost as segregating iff $k_i'=0$,

${\rm Pr}[{\rm loss}\mid k_i]=f^{k_i}>0$ ,

$E[\hat S]=\sum_i[1-f^{k_i}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true}$

for every finite $n$ because $f>0$ and $k_i<\infty$. Hence

$E[\hat\theta_W]=E[\hat S]/a_n<S_{\rm true}/a_n$

i.e. a strictly negative finite sample expectation. In the infinite-sites limit

$E[S_{\rm missed}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$

whereas $S_{\rm true}=\theta a_n\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$, so the relative loss is $O(1/\log n)$ and $E[\hat\theta_W]/\theta=1-[-\ln(1-f)]/a_n+o(a_n^{-1})\to1$. That is asymptotic consistency.

The statement in the question is about the calculation actually performed from the filtered, reference-imputed VCFs. “Arbitrarily large’’ is not infinite. For any finite, however large, $n$ the $f^{k_i}$ term is $>0$ and $E[\hat S]<S_{\rm true}$, so $\hat\theta_W$ is downward biased in the ordinary expected-value sense, the usual singleton loss $-\theta\ln(1-f)$. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition applies before per-sample quality filtering; after filtering all ALT copies at a rare site can be removed and the site is then imputed to monomorphic reference.

$\pi$ is already conceded to be systematically biased by reference imputation. With the strict finite-sample definition of bias used by the answer choices both summaries are biased in the data as described. That is the literal C reading. The B statement is the asymptotic $n\to\infty$ limit in which the $O(1)$ absolute loss of segregating sites becomes $O(1/\log n)$ relative and $\theta_W$ is recovered on the ascertained variable-site panel while $\pi$ remains permanently $1-f$ attenuated.

6.text:
I stay with C on the literal reading of the calculation that is actually performed.

With per-haplotype quality thinning followed by reference imputation a true
reference copy is always seen as reference and a true derived copy is seen
as derived w.p. $1-f>0$ and forced to reference w.p. $f>0$ independently.
For a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$ 

and 
$E[\hat d\mid p]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)$.

$\pi$ is the frequency weighted mean of $2\hat p(1-\hat p)$. The $p\to
p(1-f)$ attenuation is genotype independent and $n$ independent, so

$E[\hat\pi_i\mid p_i>0]<\pi_i$ for every $p_i>0$

and the downward $O(f)$ bias persists for any $n$ and in the $n\to\infty$
limit. Reference imputation removes derived dosage, $\pi$ is systematically
downward biased.

Watterson uses presence/absence only, $\hat\theta_W=\hat S/a_n$.
On the union VCF panel every scored site has $p_i>0$ before filtering.
For a true site with $k=2np>0$ derived copies $k'\sim{\rm Bin}(k,1-f)$
survive filtering and the site is lost as segregating iff $k'=0$,

${\rm Pr}[{\rm loss}\mid k]=f^{k}>0$,

$E[\hat S]=\sum_i[1-f^{k_i}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true}$,

so for every finite $n$ and finite $a_n$

$E[\hat\theta_W]=E[\hat S]/a_n<S_{\rm true}/a_n$.

Equivalently $E[\hat\theta_W]/\theta=1-[-\ln(1-f)]/a_n+o(a_n^{-1})<1$
for every finite $n$. The expected number of sites lost is
$E[S_{\rm missed}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$,
i.e. the usual singleton loss. It is $O(1/\log n)$ relative to
$S_{\rm true}\sim\theta\log n$ and vanishes relatively as $n\to\infty$,
hence $\hat\theta_W$ is consistent/asymptotically unbiased on the
ascertained variable-site panel. It is not unbiased for the finite VCF
that is actually analysed.

“No completely missing SNV across all samples’’ is a pre-filtering
ascertainment statement. After per-sample quality filtering all ALT copies
at a rare site can be removed and reference imputed, making the site
monomorphic in the analysed sequences. That is exactly the $f^{k}>0$ loss
above.

Hence on the filtered, reference-imputed sequences actually produced, both
frequency-weighted $\pi$ and $S$-based $\hat\theta_W$ have $E[\cdot]<\cdot$
for every finite sample size, even an arbitrarily large one. The
$O(1/\log n)$ relative bias of $\hat\theta_W$ is non-zero finite-sample
bias; consistency is not unbiasedness. That is the literal C statement.
The textbook $S$ vs frequency distinction is the asymptotic consistency of
$\hat\theta_W$ versus the permanent $1-f$ attenuation of $\pi$.

Reference imputation is genotype dependent thinning.

A true reference haplotype is always seen as reference, a true derived haplotype is seen as derived with probability $1-f>0$ and is forced to reference with probability $f>0$, independently across haplotypes. For a true derived frequency $p>0$

$E[\hat p\mid p]=p(1-f)<p$,

$E[\hat d\mid p]=2p(1-f)[1-p(1-f)]<2p(1-p)$.

$\pi$ is the frequency weighted mean of the site-wise pairwise differences. The $p\to p(1-f)$ attenuation is $n$ independent. Hence for every site with $p_i>0$

$E[\hat\pi_i\mid p_i]<\pi_i$

and the downward $O(f)$ bias does not disappear with $n$. Reference imputation systematically removes derived dosage, $\pi$ is permanently systematically downward biased.

For Watterson, $\hat\theta_W=\hat S/a_n$. On the union VCF panel every scored site has $p_i>0$ before filtering. With $k_i=2np_i>0$ true derived copies $k_i'\sim{\rm Bin}(k_i,1-f)$ survive filtering and the site is lost as segregating iff $k_i'=0$,

${\rm Pr}[{\rm loss}\mid k_i]=f^{k_i}>0$ ,

$E[\hat S]=\sum_i[1-f^{k_i}]=S_{\rm true}-\sum_i f^{k_i}<S_{\rm true}$

for every finite $n$ because $f>0$ and $k_i<\infty$. Hence

$E[\hat\theta_W]=E[\hat S]/a_n<S_{\rm true}/a_n$

i.e. a strictly negative finite sample expectation. In the infinite-sites limit

$E[S_{\rm missed}]=\theta\sum_{k\ge1}f^{k}/k=-\theta\ln(1-f)=O(1)$

whereas $S_{\rm true}=\theta a_n\sim\theta\log n\to\infty$, so the relative loss is $O(1/\log n)$ and $E[\hat\theta_W]/\theta=1-[-\ln(1-f)]/a_n+o(a_n^{-1})\to1$. That is asymptotic consistency.

The statement in the question is about the calculation actually performed from the filtered, reference-imputed VCFs. “Arbitrarily large’’ is not infinite. For any finite, however large, $n$ the $f^{k_i}$ term is $>0$ and $E[\hat S]<S_{\rm true}$, so $\hat\theta_W$ is downward biased in the ordinary expected-value sense, the usual singleton loss $-\theta\ln(1-f)$. The “no completely missing SNV across all samples’’ condition applies before per-sample quality filtering; after filtering all ALT copies at a rare site can be removed and the site is then imputed to monomorphic reference.

$\pi$ is already conceded to be systematically biased by reference imputation. With the strict finite-sample definition of bias used by the answer choices both summaries are biased in the data as described. That is the literal C reading. The B statement is the asymptotic $n\to\infty$ limit in which the $O(1)$ absolute loss of segregating sites becomes $O(1/\log n)$ relative and $\theta_W$ is recovered on the ascertained variable-site panel while $\pi$ remains permanently $1-f$ attenuated.
